title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 57 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 419–422 (Night 57, continuing directly from nights-56), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition's Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor's slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 57 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. In the Damascus slave market the merchant learns from Nuzhat al-Zamān that her name has changed from “Delight of the Age” to “Sorrow of the Age”; the Bedouin strikes her, and the merchant, moved to rescue her, haggles the Bedouin up to a hundred thousand dinars. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّابِعَةُ وَالْخَمْسُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sābiʿatu wa-al-khamsūna
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the seventh and fifty.
sentences.i: And when it was the fifty-seventh night,
sentences.n: The night-number is printed in the nominative, as a fixed formula, and the next unit supplies the speaker: "she said" (Shahrazād).

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ التَّاجِرَ تَقَدَّمَ إِلَى نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ وَهُوَ خَجْلَانُ مِنْ حُسْنِهَا وَجَمَالِهَا وَجَلَسَ إِلَى جَانِبِهَا وَقَالَ لَهَا يَاسَيِّدَتِي مَا اسْمُكِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-tājira taqaddama ilā Nuzhati al-Zamāni wa-huwa khajlānu min ḥusnihā wa-jamālihā wa-jalasa ilā jānibihā wa-qāla lahā yā-sayyidatī mā ismuki
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the fortunate-one, that the merchant advanced to Nuzhat al-Zamān, and he abashed by her beauty and her loveliness, and sat at her side and said to her: O my lady, what your name?
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the merchant approached Nuzhat al-Zamān, abashed before her beauty and loveliness, and sat down beside her and said to her, "My lady, what is your name?"
sentences.n: The merchant is the one who is about to try to buy her from the Bedouin. خَجْلَانُ is a pattern like عَطْشَانُ "thirsty" and is diptote; here it is a circumstantial clause, "he being abashed". مَا اسْمُكِ is the nominal question "what [is] your name", with no verb; the pointing -ki marks that she is addressed as a woman.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ تَسْأَلُ عَنِ اسْمِي الْيَوْمَ أَوْ قَبْلَ ذٰلِكَ الْيَوْمِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu tasʾalu ʿan ismī al-yawma aw qabla dhālika al-yawmi
sentences.l: And she said to him: You ask about my name today, or before that day?
sentences.i: She answered, "Are you asking after my name today, or the name I had before that day?"
sentences.n: There is no question particle: the question is carried by tone alone, a normal feature of spoken-style Arabic that you will meet again at once in the next line.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا أَنْتِ لَكِ اسْمٌ الْيَوْمَ وَقَبْلَ ذٰلِكَ الْيَوْمِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā anti laki ismun al-yawma wa-qabla dhālika al-yawmi
sentences.l: And he said to her: You, to-you a name today and before that day?
sentences.i: He said to her, "Have you one name today and another before that day?"
sentences.n: Again an unmarked question. The print writes only the consonants, so أَنْتِ and لَكِ are our reading, with the feminine ending, since she is the one addressed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ نَعَمْ اسْمِي قَبْلَ ذٰلِكَ الْيَوْمِ نُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ وَاسْمِي الْيَوْمَ غُصَّةُ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: qālat naʿam ismī qabla dhālika al-yawmi Nuzhatu al-Zamāni wa-ismī al-yawma Ghuṣṣatu al-Zamāni
sentences.l: She said: Yes. My name before that day: Nuzhat al-Zamān; and my name today: Ghuṣṣat al-Zamān.
sentences.i: She said, "Yes. Before that day my name was Nuzhat al-Zamān, 'Delight of the Age'; today my name is Ghuṣṣat al-Zamān, 'Sorrow of the Age.'"
sentences.n: The names are a matched pair: نُزْهَة is a pleasure-outing, a delight; غُصَّة is a lump in the throat, what chokes one. The words al-Zamān, "the Age" or "Time", are the same in both. Her answer is two verbless sentences, each "my name [is] ...".

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ التَّاجِرُ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ مِنْهَا تَغَرْغَرَتْ عَيْنَاهُ بِالدُّمُوعِ وَقَالَ لَهَا هَلْ لَكِ أَخٌ ضَعِيفٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-tājiru hādhā al-kalāma minhā taghargharat ʿaynāhu bi-al-dumūʿi wa-qāla lahā hal laki akhun ḍaʿīfun
sentences.l: And when the merchant heard this speech from her, his two eyes brimmed with the tears, and he said to her: Is there to-you a brother, weak?
sentences.i: When the merchant heard these words from her, his eyes filled with tears, and he said to her, "Have you a brother who is ailing?"
sentences.n: هَلْ لَكِ أَخٌ is "is there to you a brother", the usual way Arabic says "have you a brother". ضَعِيفٌ is "weak", and by extension frail or sick; the print uses it of her brother both here and below.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ إِي وَاللَّهِ يَاسَيِّدِى وَلٰكِنْ فَرَّقَ الزَّمَانُ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَهُ وَهُوَ مَرِيضٌ فِي بَيْتِ الْمَقْدِسِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat ī wa-Allāhi yā-sayyidī wa-lākin farraqa al-zamānu baynī wa-baynahu wa-huwa marīḍun fī bayti al-maqdisi
sentences.l: And she said: Yes, by God, O my lord, but Time parted between me and between him, and he is sick in the house of the sanctuary.
sentences.i: She said, "Yes, by God, my lord, but fate has parted him and me, and he lies sick in Jerusalem."
sentences.n: إِي is the affirmative "yes", not أَيْ "that is". بَيْتُ الْمَقْدِسِ, "the house of the sanctuary", is a name of Jerusalem. The print spells the ending of يَاسَيِّدِى with ى, as a dotless yā; we read it as ordinary -ī. Note that she calls him "lord", the form of address one uses to a man.

sentences.t: فَتَحَيَّرَ عَقْلُهُ مِنْ عُذُوبَةِ مَنْطِقِهَا وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ لَقَدْ صَدَقَ الْبَدَوِيُّ فِي مَقَالَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-taḥayyara ʿaqluhu min ʿudhūbati manṭiqihā wa-qāla fī nafsihi laqad ṣadaqa al-badawiyyu fī maqālatihi
sentences.l: And his mind was bewildered at the sweetness of her speech, and he said in himself: Indeed the Bedouin spoke truly in his saying.
sentences.i: His mind was dazed by the sweetness of her speech, and he said to himself, "The Bedouin spoke the truth in what he said."
sentences.n: قَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ, "he said in himself", is the idiom for silent thought. We do not say here which words of the Bedouin's he has in mind; the text does not repeat them.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَنَّ نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ تَذَكَّرَتْ أَخَاهَا وَمَرَضَهُ وَغُرْبَتَهُ وَفِرَاقَهَا مِنْهُ وَهُوَ ضَعِيفٌ وَلَا تَعْلَمُ مَا وَقَعَ لَهُ وَتَذَكَّرَتْ كَيْفَ مَاجَرَى لَهَا هٰذَا الْأَمْرُ مَعَ الْبَدَوِيِّ وَبُعْدِهَا عَنْ أُمِّهَا وَأَبِيهَا وَمَمْلَكَتِهَا فَجَرَتْ دُمُوعُهَا عَلَى خَدِّهَا وَأَرْسَلَتِ الْعَبَرَاتِ
sentences.tr: thumma anna Nuzhata al-Zamāni tadhakkarat akhāhā wa-maraḍahu wa-ghurbatahu wa-firāqahā minhu wa-huwa ḍaʿīfun wa-lā taʿlamu mā waqaʿa lahu wa-tadhakkarat kayfa mājarā lahā hādhā al-amru maʿa al-badawiyyi wa-buʿdahā ʿan ummihā wa-abīhā wa-mamlakatihā fa-jarat dumūʿuhā ʿalā khaddihā wa-arsalati al-ʿabarāti
sentences.l: Then indeed Nuzhat al-Zamān remembered her brother, and his sickness, and his exile, and her parting from him, and he weak, and she not knowing what had befallen him; and she remembered how this affair had happened to her with the Bedouin, and her distance from her mother and her father and her kingdom; so her tears ran on her cheek, and she sent forth the tear-drops.
sentences.i: Then Nuzhat al-Zamān remembered her brother, his illness and his exile, and how she had been parted from him while he was so frail, not knowing what had become of him. She remembered, too, how this thing had befallen her at the hands of the Bedouin, and how far she was from her mother and father and her kingdom. Her tears ran down her cheek, and she let the teardrops fall.
sentences.n: ثُمَّ أَنَّ, "then indeed", is the narrator's stock way of moving on to a new turn. مَاجَرَى is printed as one word, مَا جَرَى, "what/how it happened". The four nouns after تَذَكَّرَتْ and the further nouns joined to وَبُعْدِهَا (her mother, her father, her kingdom) are all objects of "remembered"; the sentence runs on in the print's loose style with no break.

sentences.t: وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَ—اتَ
sentences.tr: wa-anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And she recited, saying these verses.
sentences.i: And she recited these verses:
sentences.n: The archive prints الابي—ات with a dash splitting the word (a printer's line-break slip); we keep it as printed and read it as الْأَبْيَاتَ, "the verses" (the usual form is الأبيات), accusative as the object of "saying". The verses follow in the next slice.

sentences.t:
حَيْثُمَا كُنْتَ قَدْ وَقَاكَ اِلٰهِي * اَيُّهَا الرَّاحِلُ الْمُقِيمُ بِقَلْبِي
وَلَكَ اللّٰهُ حَيْثُ اَمْسَيْتَ جَارُ * حَافِظُ مِنْ صُرُوفِ دَهْرٍ وَخَطْبِ
غِبْتَ فَاسْتَوْحَشَتْ لِقُرْبِكَ عَيْنِي * وَاسْتَهَلَّتْ مَدَامِعِي اَيَّ سَكْبِ
لَيْتَ شِعْرِي بِاَيِّ رَبْعٍ وَاَرْضٍ * اَنْتَ مُسْتَوْطِنٌ بِدَارٍ وَشِعْبِ
اِنْ تَكُنْ شَارِبًا لِمَاءِ حَيَوةٍ * خَضِرُ الْوِرْدِ فَالْمَدَامِعُ شِرْبِي
اِنْ شَهِدْتَ الرُّقَادَ يَوْمًا فَجَمْرٌ * مِنْ سُهَادِي بَيْنَ الْفِرَاشِ وَجَنْبِي
كُلُّ شَيْءٍ اِلاَّ فِرَاقُكَ سَهْلٌ * عِنْدَ قَلْبِي وَغَيْرُهُ غَيْرُ صَعْبِ
sentences.tr:
ḥaythumā kunta qad waqāka ilāhī * ayyuhā al-rāḥilu al-muqīmu bi-qalbī
wa-laka allāhu ḥaythu amsayta jāru * ḥāfiẓu min ṣurūfi dahrin wa-khaṭbi
ghibta fa-istawḥashat li-qurbika ʿaynī * wa-istahallat madāmiʿī ayya sakbi
layta shiʿrī bi-ayyi rabʿin wa-arḍin * anta mustawṭinun bi-dārin wa-shiʿbi
in takun shāriban li-māʾi ḥayawatin * khaḍiru al-wirdi fa-al-madāmiʿu shirbī
in shahidta al-ruqāda yawman fa-jamrun * min suhādī bayna al-firāshi wa-janbī
kullu shayʾin illā firāquka sahlun * ʿinda qalbī wa-ghayruhu ghayru ṣaʿbi
sentences.l:
Wherever you are, indeed has-guarded-you my God, * O departing-one, the dweller in my heart.
And for you God is, wherever you spend-the-evening, a neighbour, * a guardian from the turnings of time and calamity.
You were-absent, so my eye grew-desolate for your nearness, * and my tears began-to-pour — what a pouring!
Would-that my knowing: in what dwelling and land * are you settled, in a house and a mountain-path?
If you are a drinker of the water of life, * fresh the watering-place, then the tears are my drink.
If you witness sleep one day, then a live-coal * of my sleeplessness is between the bedding and my side.
Everything except your parting is easy * to my heart, and other-than-it is not hard.
sentences.i:
Wherever you are, may my God have kept you safe, you who have left yet dwell within my heart.
And may God be your protector wherever evening finds you, a guardian against the blows of time and calamity.
You went away, and my eye grew desolate for want of you, and my tears streamed down, how they streamed!
If only I knew in what dwelling and land you now abide, in a house or a mountain pass.
If you are drinking the water of life from a fresh spring, then my tears are my drink.
If you ever see sleep, know that between my bedding and my side there lies a live coal of wakefulness.
Everything but your parting is easy to my heart, and nothing else is hard.
sentences.n: Every verse line is pointed in the print, and we copy the points exactly. جَارُ and حَافِظُ are printed without tanwīn (the poet drops it for the metre or in pausal style), and أَيَّ سَكْبِ is the exclamatory "what a pouring!" (literally "which pouring"). خَضِرُ الْوِرْدِ is printed as a nominative absolute, "fresh of watering-place". In the fifth line شِرْبِي "my drink" is the predicate: the tears are what she drinks.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ التَّاجِرُ مَا قَالَتْهُ مِنَ الشِّعْرِ بَكَى وَمَدَّيَدَهُ لِيَمْسَحَ دُمُوعَهَا عَنْ خَدِّهَا فَغَطَّتْ وَجْهَهَا وَقَالَتْ لَهُ حَاشَاكَ يَاسَيِّدِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-tājiru mā qālathu mina al-shiʿri bakā wa-maddayadahu li-yamsaḥa dumūʿahā ʿan khaddihā fa-ghaṭṭat wajhahā wa-qālat lahu ḥāshāka yā-sayyidī
sentences.l: And when the merchant heard what she had said of the poetry, he wept, and he-stretched-his-hand to wipe her tears from her cheek; so she covered her face and said to him: Far-be-it from you, O my lord.
sentences.i: When the merchant heard the verses she had spoken, he wept and reached out his hand to wipe the tears from her cheek. She covered her face and said to him, "Heaven forbid, my lord!"
sentences.n: The print writes وَمَدَّيَدَهُ as one word; read وَمَدَّ يَدَهُ, "and he stretched out his hand" (the shadda is ours, since the two words share the printed dal and yā). Likewise يَاسَيِّدِي is يَا سَيِّدِي. حَاشَاكَ is a polite refusal, "far be it from you" (literally "exempt you"): she means he must not touch her.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْبَدَوِيَّ قَعَلَ يَنْظُرُ إِلَيْهَا وَهِيَ تُغَطِّي وَجْهَهَا مِنَ التَّاجِرِ حَيْثُ أَرَادَأَنْ يَمْسَحَ دَمْعَهَا عَنْ خَدِّهَا فَاعْتَقَدَ أَنَّهَا تَمْنَعُهُ مِنَ التَّقْلِيبِ فَقَامَ إِلَيْهَا يَجْرِي وَكَانَ مَعَهُ مِقْوَدُ جَمَلٍ فَشَالَهُ فِي يَدِهِ وَضَرَبَهَا بِهِ عَلَي أَكْتَافِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-badawiyya qaʿala yanẓuru ilayhā wa-hiya tughaṭṭī wajhahā mina al-tājiri ḥaythu arāda an yamsaḥa damʿahā ʿan khaddihā fa-iʿtaqada annahā tamnaʿuhu mina al-taqlībi fa-qāma ilayhā yajrī wa-kāna maʿahu miqwadu jamalin fa-shālahu fī yadihi wa-ḍarabahā bihi ʿalā aktāfihā
sentences.l: Then indeed the Bedouin, he-sat(?) looking at her while she was covering her face from the merchant, since he wanted that he wipe her tear from her cheek; so he believed that she was refusing him the handling, and he rose to her running; and with him was a camel's halter-rope, so he lifted it in his hand, and struck her with it upon her shoulders.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the Bedouin sat watching her cover her face from the merchant, because the merchant had wanted to wipe the tear from her cheek. He took it that she was refusing the handling, and he leapt up and ran at her. He had a camel's halter-rope with him, and he raised it in his hand and struck her across the shoulders with it.
sentences.n: قَعَلَ is printed so, and we keep it. It is probably a misprint for قَعَدَ "he sat" or جَعَلَ "he began"; either way it governs the participle-like يَنْظُرُ ("sat looking" or "began looking"). أَرَادَأَنْ is one printed word, "he wanted to". حَيْثُ here means "since, because" (a Middle Arabic use), not "where". التَّقْلِيبُ is the turning-over or handling of a slave girl by a buyer. عَلَي is printed with a dotted yā for عَلَى. The Bedouin takes her covering of her face as a refusal to be inspected for sale.

sentences.t: فَجَاءَتِ الضَّرْبَةُ بِقُوَّةٍ فَانْكَبَّتْ بِوَجْهِهَا عَلَى الْأَرْضِ فَجَاءَتْ حَصَاةٌ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ فِي حَاجِبِهَا فَشَقَّتْهُ فَسَالَ دَمُهَا عَلَى وَجْهِهَا فَصَرَخَتْ صَرْخَةً عَظِيمَةً وَغُشِيَ عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-jāʾati al-ḍarbatu bi-quwwatin fa-inkabbat bi-wajhihā ʿalā al-arḍi fa-jāʾat ḥaṣātun mina al-arḍi fī ḥājibihā fa-shaqqathu fa-sāla damuhā ʿalā wajhihā fa-ṣarakhat ṣarkhatan ʿaẓīmatan wa-ghushiya ʿalayhā
sentences.l: So the blow came with force, and she fell-forward with her face upon the ground; and a pebble from the ground came into her eyebrow and split it, so her blood flowed over her face, and she cried out a great cry, and it-was-fainted upon her.
sentences.i: The blow fell hard, and she pitched forward onto the ground on her face. A pebble from the ground struck her brow and split it, and the blood ran down her face. She screamed aloud and fainted away.
sentences.n: وَغُشِيَ عَلَيْهَا (passive, "it was covered over upon her") is the idiom for "she swooned"; the verb is impersonal, so it does not agree with her. بِوَجْهِهَا is "on her face" (bi- of accompaniment: she fell with her face to the ground).

sentences.t: وَبَكَتْ وَبَكَى التَّاجِرُ مَعَهَا فَقَالَ التَّاجِرُ لَا بُدَّأَنْ أَشْتَرِيَ هٰذِهِ الْجَارِيَةَ وَلَوْ بِثِقْلِهَا ذَهَبًا وَأُرِيحَهَا مِنْ هٰذَا الظَّالِمِ
sentences.tr: wa-bakat wa-bakā al-tājiru maʿahā fa-qāla al-tājiru lā budda an ashtariya hādhihi al-jāriyata wa-law bi-thiqlihā dhahaban wa-urīḥahā min hādhā al-ẓālimi
sentences.l: And she wept, and the merchant wept with her; and the merchant said: There-is-no-escape that I buy this slave-girl, even with her weight in gold, and that I relieve her of this wrongdoer.
sentences.i: She wept, and the merchant wept with her. Then the merchant said, "I must buy this girl, even if I pay her weight in gold, and rescue her from this brute."
sentences.n: لَا بُدَّ أَنْ (printed as one word, لَا بُدَّأَنْ) is "it is unavoidable that", i.e. "I must"; it takes the subjunctive, here أَشْتَرِيَ and أُرِيحَهَا. وَلَوْ بِثِقْلِهَا ذَهَبًا is "even at her weight, in gold": بِـ is the price paid, ثِقْل is weight, and ذَهَبًا is an accusative of specification. مِنْ هٰذَا الظَّالِمِ: مِنْ marks what she is relieved of.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ التَّاجِرُ يَشْتُمُ الْبَدَوِيَّ وَهِيَ فِي غَشْيَتِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra al-tājiru yashtumu al-badawiyya wa-hiya fī ghashyatihā
sentences.l: And the merchant began reviling the Bedouin while she was in her swoon.
sentences.i: The merchant began cursing the Bedouin while she lay in her swoon.
sentences.n: صَارَ followed by a present verb means "began to". وَهِيَ فِي غَشْيَتِهَا is a circumstantial clause, "while she was in her swoon".

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَفَاقَتْ مَسَحَتِ الدُّمُوعَ وَالدَّمَ عَنْ وَجْهِهَا وَعَصَبَتْ رَأْسَهَا وَرَفَعَتْ طَرْفَهَا إِلَى السَّمَاءِ وَطَلَبَتْ مِنْ مَوْلَاهَا بِقَلْبٍ حَزِينٍ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ شِعْرًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā afāqat masaḥati al-dumūʿa wa-al-dama ʿan wajhihā wa-ʿaṣabat raʾsahā wa-rafaʿat ṭarfahā ilā al-samāʾi wa-ṭalabat min mawlāhā bi-qalbin ḥazīnin wa-anshadat taqūlu shiʿran
sentences.l: And when she revived, she wiped the tears and the blood from her face, and bound her head, and raised her glance to the sky, and asked of her Lord with a sorrowful heart, and recited, saying poetry:
sentences.i: When she came to, she wiped the tears and the blood from her face, bandaged her head, and lifted her gaze to heaven. With a sorrowing heart she made her petition to her Lord, and she recited these verses:
sentences.n: مَوْلَاهَا is "her master" and here means God. وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ شِعْرًا is "she recited, saying poetry": تَقُولُ is redundant, a stock introduction to verse. طَلَبَتْ مِنْ is "asked of".

sentences.t:
وَا رَحْمَتَا لِعَزِيْزَهِ * بِالضَّيْمِ قَدْ صَارَتْ ذَلِيلَهْ
تَبْكِي بِدَمْعٍ هَاطِلٍ * وَتَقُولُ مَا فِي الْوَغْدِ حِيلَهْ
sentences.tr:
wā raḥmatā li-ʿazīzahi * bi-al-ḍaymi qad ṣārat dhalīlah
tabkī bi-damʿin hāṭilin * wa-taqūlu mā fī al-waghdi ḥīlah
sentences.l: O pity for a dear-one, / by wrong she has become abased; / she weeps with a pouring tear / and says: "in the vile-one there is no ruse."
sentences.i: Oh, the pity of it, for a cherished woman / brought low by cruel wrong, / weeping with streaming tears, / and saying, "There is no trick to be had against the wretch."
sentences.n: Nuzhat al-Zamān's verses, in which she speaks of herself in the third person. The pointing is the edition's own and is kept as printed, including the pausal -ah rhyme (ذَلِيلَهْ, حِيلَهْ) and the kasra on the final h of لِعَزِيْزَهِ, which reads li-ʿazīzahi: the poem is in a loose, near-colloquial register. الْوَغْدِ "the vile one" is the Bedouin.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَتْ مِنْ شِعْرِهَا الْتَفَتَتْ إِلَى التَّاجِرِ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ بِصَوْتٍ خَفِيٍّ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghat min shiʿrihā iltafatat ilā al-tājiri wa-qālat lahu bi-ṣawtin khafiyyin
sentences.l: And when she had finished from her poetry, she turned to the merchant and said to him with a hidden voice:
sentences.i: When she had finished her verses, she turned to the merchant and said to him in a low voice,

sentences.t: بِاللَّهِ لَا تَدَعْنِي عِنْدَ هَذَا الظَّالِمِ الَّذِي لَا يَعْرِفُ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى فَإِنِّي إِنْ بِتُّ هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةَ عِنْدَهُ قَتَلْتُ نَفْسِي بِيَدِي فَخَلِّصْنِي مِنْهُ يُخَلِّصْكَ اللَّهُ مِنْ نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ
sentences.tr: bi-allāhi lā tadaʿnī ʿinda hādhā al-ẓālimi alladhī lā yaʿrifu allāha taʿālā fa-innī in bittu hādhihi al-laylata ʿindahu qataltu nafsī bi-yadī fa-khalliṣnī minhu yukhalliṣka allāhu min nāri jahannama
sentences.l: By God, do not leave me with this wrongdoer who does not know God, exalted; for if I spend-the-night this night with him, I (will) have killed my self with my hand. So deliver me from him; God will deliver you from the fire of Gehenna.
sentences.i: By God, do not leave me with this tyrant, who does not know God Most High. If I spend this night with him, I will kill myself with my own hand. Rescue me from him, and God will rescue you from the fire of Hell.
sentences.n: The perfect قَتَلْتُ after إِنْ is a conditional with future sense ("I will have killed"). يُخَلِّصْكَ is the jussive that follows an imperative: "do this, and then ...". جَهَنَّمَ (Gehenna, Hell) is diptote.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ التَّاجِرُ وَقَالَ لِلْبَدَوِيِّ يَا شَيْخَ الْعَرَبِ هَذِهِ لَيْسَتْ غَرَضَكَ بِعْنِي إِيَّاهَا بِمَا تُرِيدُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-tājiru wa-qāla li-al-badawiyyi yā shaykha al-ʿarabi hādhihi laysat gharaḍaka biʿnī iyyāhā bi-mā turīdu
sentences.l: So the merchant stood and said to the Bedouin: "O sheikh of the Arabs, this one is not your aim; sell me her for what you want."
sentences.i: The merchant rose and said to the Bedouin, "Sheikh of the Arabs, she is not what you are after. Sell her to me for whatever price you name."
sentences.n: هَذِهِ لَيْسَتْ غَرَضَكَ is elliptical: literally "this (woman) is not your aim/purpose", i.e. not what you want her for, or not worth keeping; the sense is evident, the exact intent a little loose. Note the doubled pronoun object بِعْنِي إِيَّاهَا "sell me her", and بِمَا تُرِيدُ "for what you want", where بِـ marks the price.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْبَدَوِيُّ خُذْهَا وَادْفَعْ ثَمَنَهَا وَإِلَّا أَرُوحُ بِهَا إِلَى النَّجْعِ وَأُخَلِّيهَا هُنَاكَ تَلُمُّ الْبَعْرَ وَتَرْعَى الْجِمَالَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-badawiyyu khudhhā wa-idfaʿ thamanahā wa-illā arūḥu bihā ilā al-najʿi wa-ukhalliyhā hunāka talummu al-baʿra wa-tarʿā al-jimāla
sentences.l: So the Bedouin said: "Take her and pay her price, and if-not I go with her to the pasture-camp and leave her there, she gathers the dung and pastures the camels."
sentences.i: The Bedouin said, "Take her and pay her price, or else I will carry her off to the grazing camp and leave her there to gather dung and tend the camels."
sentences.n: وَإِلَّا أَرُوحُ is vocalised with the indicative as printed; strict Classical would use the jussive (أَرُحْ) after "if not". تَلُمُّ وَتَرْعَى are bare imperfects giving the state she would be in ("... she gathering dung and tending camels"). رَاحَ بِـ "go off with", with بِـ marking the one carried along. النَّجْعِ is the Bedouin pasturage, the camp's grazing ground.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ التَّاجِرُ أُعْطِيكَ خَمْسِينَ أَلْفَ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-tājiru uʿṭīka khamsīna alfa dīnārin
sentences.l: So the merchant said: "I give you fifty thousand dinars."
sentences.i: The merchant said, "I will give you fifty thousand dinars."

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْبَدَوِيُّ يَفْتَحُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-badawiyyu yaftaḥu allāhu taʿālā
sentences.l: So the Bedouin said: "God, exalted, will open."
sentences.i: The Bedouin said, "God will provide."
sentences.n: A stock brush-off to a bid ("may God open another door"): it declines the offer without arguing it. It recurs in the next unit.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ التَّاجِرُ سَبْعُونَ أَلْفَ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-tājiru sabʿūna alfa dīnārin
sentences.l: So the merchant said: "Seventy thousand dinars."
sentences.n: The bid is a bare nominative (سَبْعُونَ), not the accusative Classical would put after an understood "I give"; read it as an exclamatory price.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْبَدَوِيُّ يَفْتَحُ اللَّهُ هَذَا مَا هُوَ رَأْسُ مَالِهَا لِأَنَّهَا أَكَلَتْ عِنْدِي أَقْرَاصَ شَعِيرٍ بِتِسْعِينَ أَلْفَ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-badawiyyu yaftaḥu allāhu hādhā mā huwa raʾsu mālihā li-annahā akalat ʿindī aqrāṣa shaʿīrin bi-tisʿīna alfa dīnārin
sentences.l: So the Bedouin said: "God will open. This is not the head of her wealth, because she ate at my place discs of barley for ninety thousand dinars."
sentences.i: The Bedouin said, "God will provide. That is not even her cost to me, for she has eaten barley loaves at my place to the value of ninety thousand dinars."
sentences.n: رَأْسُ مَالِهَا ("head of her wealth") is the capital or cost-price: the Bedouin pretends the barley she ate already exceeds the bid. The absurd figure is haggling bravado. بِـ in بِتِسْعِينَ marks the value or price.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ التَّاجِرُ أَنْتَ وَأَهْلُكَ وَقَبِيلَتُكَ فِي طُولِ زَمَانِكُمْ مَا أَكَلْتُمْ بِأَلْفِ دِينَارٍ شَعِيرًا وَلَكِنْ أَنَا أَقُولُ لَكَ كَلِمَةً وَاحِدَةً فَإِنْ لَمْ تَرْضَ بِهَا غَمَزْتُ عَلَيْكَ نَائِبَ دِمَشْقَ فَيَأْخُذُهَا مِنْكَ قَهْرًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-tājiru anta wa-ahluka wa-qabīlatuka fī ṭūli zamānikum mā akaltum bi-alfi dīnārin shaʿīran wa-lākin anā aqūlu laka kalimatan wāḥidatan fa-in lam tarḍa bihā ghamaztu ʿalayka nāʾiba dimashqa fa-yaʾkhudhuhā minka qahran
sentences.l: So the merchant said to him: "You and your family and your tribe, in the length of your time, you have not eaten, for a thousand dinars, barley. But I say to you one word: if you are not pleased with it, I will have informed on you (to) the deputy of Damascus, and he takes her from you by force."
sentences.i: The merchant said to him, "You and your family and your tribe, in all your days, have never eaten a thousand dinars' worth of barley. But I will tell you one thing: if you do not accept it, I will denounce you to the governor of Damascus, and he will take her from you by force."
sentences.n: وَلَكِنْ أَنَا uses a free pronoun after "but", where Classical writes لَكِنِّي. غَمَزَ عَلَى "inform against, tip off" is a perfect with future sense after إِنْ لَمْ, like قَتَلْتُ above. نَائِبَ دِمَشْقَ is the deputy (viceroy) of Damascus; his seizure of her is the threat.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْبَدَوِيُّ تَكَلَّمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-badawiyyu takallam
sentences.l: So the Bedouin said: "Speak."

sentences.t: فَقَالَ بِمِائَةِ أَلْفِ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla bi-miʾati alfi dīnārin
sentences.l: So he said: "For a hundred thousand dinars."
sentences.n: Nobody is named: it is the merchant who answers, and بِـ marks the price ("at a hundred thousand").

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْبَدَوِيُّ بِعْتُكَ إِيَّاهَا بِهَذَا الثَّمَنِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-badawiyyu biʿtuka iyyāhā bi-hādhā al-thamani
sentences.l: So the Bedouin said: "I have sold you her for this price."
sentences.i: The Bedouin said, "I have sold her to you at this price."
sentences.n: The perfect بِعْتُكَ makes the sale by being said, the formula that closes a bargain. Printed هذا الثمن is kept; بِـ marks the price.

sentences.t: وَاقْدُرْ أَٔنَّنِي اشْتَرَيْتُ بِهَا مِلْحًا
sentences.tr: wa-uqdur annanī ishtaraytu bihā milḥan
sentences.l: And reckon that-I bought with-her salt.
sentences.i: And suppose that I bought salt with it.
sentences.n: The Bedouin's speech continues from the previous unit, still addressed to the merchant. وَاقْدُرْ is read as an imperative "reckon, suppose" (the print has no points, so this is our best reading). بِهَا is feminine singular, "with her/it", and could refer to the girl or to a coin; the sense is uncertain, and we keep the literal "with-her".

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَهُ التَّاجِرُ ضَحِكَ وَمَضَى إِٔلَى مَنْزِلِهِ وَأَٔتَى لَهُ بِالْمَالِ وَأَٔقْبَضَهُ إِٔيَّاهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿahu al-tājiru ḍaḥika wa-maḍā ilā manzilihi wa-atā lahu bi-al-māli wa-aqbaḍahu iyyāhu
sentences.l: And when heard-him the merchant, he-laughed, and he-went to his-dwelling, and he-came to-him with the money, and he-made-him-take-possession-of it.
sentences.i: When the merchant heard this he laughed, went off to his house, and came back to him with the money, which he handed over to him.
sentences.n: أَتَى لَهُ بِالْمَالِ is "he brought him the money": أَتَى بِـ takes the thing brought and لَهُ the person it is brought to. أَقْبَضَهُ إِيَّاهُ (form IV) is "made him take hold of it", with both objects, the second carried by the pronoun إِيَّاهُ.

sentences.t: فَأَٔخَذَهُ الْبَدَوِيُّ فَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhahu al-badawiyyu fa-qāla fī nafsihi
sentences.l: And took-it the Bedouin, and he-said in his-self:
sentences.i: The Bedouin took it and said to himself,

sentences.t: لَا بُدَّأنْ أَٔذْهَبَ إِٔلَى الْقُدْسِ لَعَلِّي أَٔجِدَ أَٔخَاهَا فَأَٔجِيءَ بِهِ وَأَٔبِيعَهُ
sentences.tr: lā budda an adhhaba ilā al-quds laʿallī ajida akhāhā fa-ajīʾa bihi wa-abīʿahu
sentences.l: No escape that I go to Jerusalem; perhaps-I find her-brother, and I-bring with-him and I-sell-him.
sentences.i: I must go to Jerusalem; perhaps I shall find her brother, bring him back, and sell him.
sentences.n: The print runs لَا بُدَّ and أَنْ together as one word, بدان; we read لَا بُدَّ أَنْ, "there is no escaping that", that is, "I must". جَاءَ بِهِ is "bring (him)", the verb choosing بِـ. Notice the plan: the Bedouin means to sell the girl's brother as a slave too.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَكِبَ وَسَافَرَ إِٔلَى أَٔنْ وَصَلَ إِٔلَى بَيْتِ الْمَقْدِسِ فَذَهَبَ إِٔلَى الْخَانِ وَسَأَلَ عَنْ أَٔخِيهَا فَلَمْ يَجِدْهُ
sentences.tr: thumma rakiba wa-sāfara ilā an waṣala ilā bayti al-maqdisi fa-dhahaba ilā al-khāni wa-saʾala ʿan akhīhā fa-lam yajidhu
sentences.l: Then he-mounted and travelled until that he-arrived at house-of the-sanctuary, and he-went to the inn, and he-asked about her-brother, and not he-found-him.
sentences.i: Then he mounted and travelled until he reached Jerusalem. He went to the inn and asked after her brother, but did not find him.
sentences.n: بَيْتُ الْمَقْدِسِ, "the house of the sanctuary", is the usual name for Jerusalem; the Bedouin's earlier word الْقُدْسِ is the same city. إِلَى أَنْ is "until".

sentences.t: هَذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَٔمْرِهِ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amrihi
sentences.l: This, what was of his-affair.
sentences.i: So much for him.
sentences.n: A stock transition: the narrator closes one thread ("that is what became of him") before turning to the other.

sentences.t: وَأَٔمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَٔمْرِ التَّاجِرِ وَنُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ فَإِٔنَّهُ لَمَّا أَٔخَذَهَا أَلْقَى عَلَيْهَا شَيْأً مِنْ قُمَاشِهِ وَمَضَى بِهَا إِٔلَى مَنْزِلِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri al-tājiri wa-Nuzhati al-Zamāni fa-innahu lammā akhadhahā alqā ʿalayhā shayʾan min qumāshihi wa-maḍā bihā ilā manzilihi
sentences.l: And as-for what was of the-affair-of the merchant and Nuzhat al-Zamān, then-indeed-he, when he-took her, he-cast upon-her something of his-cloth and he-went with-her to his-dwelling.
sentences.i: As for the merchant and Nuzhat al-Zamān, when he had taken her he threw some of his clothing over her and went with her to his house.
sentences.n: وَأَمَّا ... فَإِنَّهُ is the standard "as for X, he ..." frame: فَـ answers أَمَّا. قُمَاشٌ is cloth or clothing; he covers her so that she is not seen in the street. مَضَى بِهَا is "went off with her", the بِـ marking the one taken along.

sentences.t: وَأَٔدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُ—بَ—احِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mu—ba—āḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she-fell-silent from the speech the permitted.
sentences.i: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech unspoken.
sentences.n: The print splits the last word with dashes, الم—ب—اح, and we keep it as printed; read al-mubāḥ. This is the stock closing formula of a night: the morning overtakes Shahrazād and she stops "the permitted speech", the story she was allowed to tell. Her name is printed here as one word.
